title: Transformations & Symmetry
description: Reflect, rotate, translate and enlarge shapes on a coordinate grid, and identify line and rotational symmetry.

notes.heading: Reflection

illustration.alt: Coordinate grid showing a triangle and its reflections, rotations, translations and enlargements.
illustration.caption: Reflections, rotations, translations and enlargements change position or size while preserving shape.

notes.body:
📌 Definition
A reflection creates a mirror image of a shape across a mirror line. Every point on the image is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line as the matching point on the original shape.

🔑 Key Concept
Common coordinate rules are:
• x-axis: $(x,y) 	o (x,-y)$
• y-axis: $(x,y) 	o (-x,y)$
• line $y=x$: $(x,y) 	o (y,x)$
For a vertical mirror line $x=a$, the $y$-coordinate stays the same and $x' = 2a - x$.
For a horizontal mirror line $y=b$, the $x$-coordinate stays the same and $y' = 2b - y$.

💡 Worked Example
Reflect point $P(5,3)$ in the line $x=2$.

Step 1: Find the horizontal distance from $P$ to the mirror line: $5 - 2 = 3$ units.
Step 2: Move the same distance on the other side: $2 - 3 = -1$.
So $P' = (-1,3)$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Reflection preserves size and shape; the image is congruent to the original.
• The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining any point to its image.
• Only the coordinate perpendicular to the mirror line changes sign; the other stays the same.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping both coordinates when reflecting in a vertical or horizontal line. For $x=a$ only $x$ changes; for $y=b$ only $y$ changes.

notes.heading: Rotation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point called the centre of rotation. A full description needs the centre, the angle and the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise).

🔑 Key Concept
When rotating around the origin $(0,0)$:
• $90^\circ$ clockwise: $(x,y) 	o (y,-x)$
• $90^\circ$ anticlockwise: $(x,y) 	o (-y,x)$
• $180^\circ$: $(x,y) 	o (-x,-y)$
A $180^\circ$ rotation has no direction because clockwise and anticlockwise give the same result.

💡 Worked Example
Rotate $A(2,3)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise around $(0,0)$.

Using the rule $(x,y) 	o (y,-x)$:
$A' = (3,-2)$.

✅ Check
The distance from $A$ to the origin should equal the distance from $A'$ to the origin.
$OA = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}$ and $OA' = \sqrt{3^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{13}$, so the answer is consistent.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing clockwise and anticlockwise. Remember that $90^\circ$ clockwise is the same as $270^\circ$ anticlockwise.

notes.heading: Translation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A translation slides a shape without rotating, reflecting or resizing it. Every point of the shape moves by the same amount in the same direction.

🔑 Key Concept
A translation is written as a column vector:
$$\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}$$
where $a$ is horizontal movement (positive to the right, negative to the left) and $b$ is vertical movement (positive up, negative down).

To find the image of a point, add the vector to the coordinates:
$$(x,y) 	o (x+a,\; y+b)$$

💡 Worked Example
A triangle has vertex $B(-1,4)$. It is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$. Find $B'$.

New $x$-coordinate: $-1 + 3 = 2$
New $y$-coordinate: $4 + (-2) = 2$
So $B' = (2,2)$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Translations preserve size, shape and orientation.
• Two translations can be combined by adding their vectors.
• The opposite vector $\begin{pmatrix} -a \\ -b \end{pmatrix}$ undoes the translation.

✅ Check
Translating by a vector and then by its opposite vector returns every point to its starting position.

notes.heading: Enlargement
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An enlargement changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre of enlargement. It produces an image that is similar to the original.

🔑 Key Concept
If the centre is the origin and the scale factor is $k$, each coordinate is multiplied by $k$:
$$(x,y) 	o (kx,\; ky)$$
• $k > 1$ makes the image larger and farther from the centre.
• $0 < k < 1$ makes the image smaller and closer to the centre.
• $k < 0$ places the image on the opposite side of the centre.

When the centre is not the origin, measure distances from the centre and multiply each distance by $k$.

💡 Worked Example
Enlarge triangle $P(1,2)$, $Q(3,2)$, $R(1,5)$ by scale factor $2$ about $(0,0)$.

$P' = (1 	imes 2,\; 2 	imes 2) = (2,4)$
$Q' = (3 	imes 2,\; 2 	imes 2) = (6,4)$
$R' = (1 	imes 2,\; 5 	imes 2) = (2,10)$

Each side length is doubled but the angles stay the same.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that the centre of enlargement may not be the origin. When the centre is a different point, you must use distances from that point, not simply multiply coordinates.

notes.heading: Line Symmetry and Rotational Symmetry
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A shape has line symmetry if it can be folded along a line so that the two halves match exactly. That line is called a line of symmetry.
A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after being rotated by less than $360^\circ$ around its centre. The number of positions that look the same is called the order of rotational symmetry.

🔑 Key Concept
• A square has $4$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $4$.
• A rectangle has $2$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $2$.
• A regular polygon with $n$ sides has $n$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $n$.

💡 Worked Example
How many lines of symmetry and what is the order of rotational symmetry for an equilateral triangle?

An equilateral triangle has $3$ lines of symmetry, one through each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. It also maps onto itself after rotations of $120^\circ$ and $240^\circ$, so its rotational symmetry order is $3$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Line symmetry is about matching halves; rotational symmetry is about matching positions after turning.
• A shape with no rotational symmetry still has order $1$, because it matches itself after a full $360^\circ$ turn.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying a shape has rotational symmetry of order $0$. Every shape matches itself after one full turn, so the minimum order is $1$.

notes.heading: Congruent and Similar Images
notes.body:
📌 Definition
• Congruent shapes have exactly the same size and shape. Corresponding sides and angles are equal.
• Similar shapes have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

🔑 Key Concept
Reflection, rotation and translation are isometries: they preserve distance, so the image is congruent to the original.
Enlargement changes lengths by the scale factor $k$, so the image is similar to the original (congruent only when $k = 1$).

💡 Worked Example
A rectangle with sides $3$ cm and $6$ cm is enlarged by scale factor $\dfrac{2}{3}$. Is the image congruent or similar?

New sides: $3 	imes \dfrac{2}{3} = 2$ cm and $6 	imes \dfrac{2}{3} = 4$ cm.
The angles are still $90^\circ$ but the sides are different lengths, so the image is similar to the original.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Congruent: same shape, same size.
• Similar: same shape, sides in proportion.
• Reflections, rotations and translations produce congruent images.
• Enlargements produce similar images.

✅ Check
Compare matching sides. If every pair is equal, the shapes are congruent; if every pair is in the same ratio, they are similar.

notes.heading: Describing and Combining Transformations
notes.body:
📌 Definition
To describe a transformation fully, you must give enough information for someone else to reproduce the image exactly.

🔑 Key Concept
Required details for each transformation:
• Reflection: state the mirror line.
• Rotation: state the centre, the angle and the direction.
• Translation: state the column vector.
• Enlargement: state the centre and the scale factor.

Some combinations can be replaced by a single transformation:
• Two reflections in parallel lines equal one translation.
• Two reflections in intersecting lines equal one rotation.
• Two translations add their vectors.

💡 Worked Example
A shape is reflected in the $x$-axis and the image is then reflected in the $y$-axis. What single transformation is this?

Step 1: Reflect $(x,y)$ in the $x$-axis: $(x,-y)$.
Step 2: Reflect the result in the $y$-axis: $(-x,-y)$.
The final rule is $(x,y) 	o (-x,-y)$, which is a $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying the second transformation to the original point instead of to the image from the first step. Always use the most recent image when combining transformations.

flashcards.definition: A transformation that produces a mirror image of a shape across a mirror line.
Turning a shape around a fixed point by a given angle and direction.
A column vector showing horizontal and vertical movement.
flashcards.example: $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ means $4$ units right and $3$ units down.

flashcards.definition: A transformation that changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre.
flashcards.example: Enlarging $(1,3)$ by scale factor $2$ about $(0,0)$ gives $(2,6)$.

flashcards.definition: The multiplier used in an enlargement.
flashcards.example: A scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ halves every side length.

flashcards.definition: The fixed point from which an enlargement is measured.
flashcards.example: Lines drawn through corresponding vertices meet at the centre of enlargement.

flashcards.definition: Exactly the same shape and size; corresponding sides and angles are equal.
flashcards.example: A shape and its reflection are congruent.

flashcards.definition: Same shape but not necessarily the same size; corresponding angles are equal and sides are in proportion.
flashcards.example: An enlargement with scale factor $3$ creates a similar shape.

flashcards.definition: A shape has line symmetry if it can be folded along a line so that the two halves match.
flashcards.example: A square has $4$ lines of symmetry.

flashcards.definition: A shape looks the same after a rotation of less than $360^\circ$.
flashcards.example: An equilateral triangle has rotational symmetry of order $3$.

flashcards.definition: The number of times a shape maps onto itself during one complete turn.
flashcards.example: A regular pentagon has rotational symmetry of order $5$.

flashcards.definition: A sequence of two or more transformations applied one after another.
flashcards.example: Reflecting in the $x$-axis then the $y$-axis is equivalent to a $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin.

questions.stem: Point $(4,5)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate: $(x,y) 	o (-x,y)$. So $(4,5) 	o (-4,5)$.

questions.stem: Point $(2,1)$ is rotated $90^\circ$ clockwise around $(0,0)$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: The rule for $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin is $(x,y) 	o (y,-x)$. Applying it to $(2,1)$ gives $(1,-2)$.

questions.stem: Point $(-3,4)$ is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$. What is the image?
questions.explanation: Add the vector to the point: $-3 + 5 = 2$ and $4 + (-2) = 2$. The image is $(2,2)$.

questions.stem: Point $(2,3)$ is enlarged by scale factor $3$ about $(0,0)$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: For an enlargement about the origin, multiply each coordinate by the scale factor: $(2 	imes 3,\; 3 	imes 3) = (6,9)$.

questions.stem: Which transformation can change the size of a shape?
questions.explanation: Only enlargement changes size. Reflections, translations and rotations produce congruent images that keep the same size.

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explanation: A square has $4$ lines of symmetry: two diagonals and the vertical and horizontal midlines.

questions.stem: Point $(6,2)$ is reflected in the line $x=1$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: The distance from $x=6$ to $x=1$ is $5$ units. Moving $5$ units to the other side gives $x = 1 - 5 = -4$. The $y$-coordinate stays $2$, so the image is $(-4,2)$.

questions.stem: A regular hexagon has rotational symmetry of which order?
questions.explanation: A regular polygon with $n$ sides has rotational symmetry of order $n$. A regular hexagon has $6$ sides, so its order is $6$.

questions.stem: Point $(-3,2)$ is rotated $180^\circ$ around $(0,0)$. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explanation: A $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin reverses both coordinates: $(x,y) 	o (-x,-y)$. So $(-3,2) 	o (3,-2)$.

questions.stem: A translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ is followed by a translation by vector $\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$. What is the single equivalent vector?
questions.explanation: Add the two vectors: $2 + (-3) = -1$ and $-1 + 4 = 3$. The single equivalent vector is $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

questions.stem: A shape is reflected in the $x$-axis and the resulting image is reflected in the $y$-axis. What single transformation is this equivalent to?
questions.explanation: Reflecting $(x,y)$ in the $x$-axis gives $(x,-y)$, and reflecting that in the $y$-axis gives $(-x,-y)$. That is exactly the rule for a $180^\circ$ rotation about the origin.

questions.stem: Which of these transformations always produces a congruent image?
questions.explanation: Reflections, rotations and translations preserve size and shape, so they always produce congruent images. Enlargements change size, so they produce similar images.

questions.stem: A triangle has vertices $(1,1)$, $(3,1)$ and $(1,4)$. It is enlarged by scale factor $-2$ about $(0,0)$. What are the coordinates of the image of $(1,1)$?
questions.explanation: A negative scale factor multiplies each coordinate by $-2$ and places the image on the opposite side of the centre: $(1 	imes -2,\; 1 	imes -2) = (-2,-2)$.

questions.stem: A butterfly has one line of symmetry down its body. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
questions.explanation: A butterfly only maps onto itself after a full $360^\circ$ turn, so its order of rotational symmetry is $1$. The minimum order for any shape is $1$.

questions.stem: Point $P(a,b)$ is reflected in the line $y=x$ and then reflected in the $y$-axis. What are the final coordinates?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in $y=x$ swaps the coordinates: $(a,b) 	o (b,a)$. Reflecting in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate: $(b,a) 	o (-b,a)$.
